name: Concentric Policies: health tax advocacy in Liberia and Guinea-Bissau (charityevals, first year 2023-24)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults: Liberia's stopped tax cut and 2025 tax act (95%), Guinea-Bissau's tobacco tax (5%).
summary: Concentric Policies, a two-founder project incubated by Ambitious Impact in 2023, advises the governments of Liberia and Guinea-Bissau on tobacco and alcohol taxes. This model counts what its first year (about October 2023 to September 2024, about $80,000 by its own account, no audited accounts) did: its report that it stopped a 2024 executive order that would have cut Liberia's alcohol and tobacco taxes (found nowhere else, so taken as a {{row:eo_p_success}} chance that the order was real and stopped, with Concentric credited {{row:eo_attribution_share_shared}} of stopping it; the alcohol part counts about a year, since the Legislature cut beverage excise in April 2025 anyway), a small share of Liberia's 2025 tax act, which raised and indexed those taxes, and a {{row:gnb_p_adopted}} chance that Guinea-Bissau applies the tobacco tax rise it passed in 2022. Each change moves prices, smoking and heavy drinking by the shared price responses, deaths are valued by age and second-hand smoke counts as a side effect. The result, about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, is dominated by judgment: whether the order was real, how much of a tax change reaches prices where excise is weakly collected, and Concentric's credit; every branch is discounted for missing data, since no change in prices or health from its work is measured, and the next dollar counts at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the average.

rows.label: Years a won (or defended) tax counts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a won policy counts before it would have come anyway (docs/normalization.md 2.9). A tax cut stopped counts the same way: the years until the same rates would have come back.

rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: tobacco): taxes take effect at once or at the next budget year. Read by the stopped executive order, which would have applied from 2024; the other branches have their own waits.

rows.label: Discounted years counted (the stopped cut)
Tobacco: discount for the wait from the price change to the health gain
rows.explainer: About half of a price rise's long-run cut in smoking comes from smokers quitting, whose gain comes about 8 years later; the rest from young people who never start, about 40 years later (shared figures, facts: tobacco), each discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Alcohol: discount for the wait from the price change to the health gain
rows.explainer: Injuries and violence fall at once, cirrhosis and cancers over years: the shared lag (facts: alcohol, 3 years), discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Tobacco: share of the smoking burden averted per 1% higher cigarette prices
rows.explainer: Shared (facts: tobacco): a price elasticity of about -0.5 in poor countries, about half of it in fewer smokers, so 0.25% of the burden per 1% of price.

rows.label: Alcohol: share of the alcohol burden averted per 1% higher alcohol prices
rows.explainer: Shared (facts: alcohol): heavy drinking's mean price elasticity, -0.28 (Wagenaar et al., 2009).

rows.label: Stopped tax cut: chance an order cutting these taxes was real, on its way to taking effect, and stopped
rows.explainer: The founders write that in 2024 they "halted an executive order in Liberia that would have decreased alcohol and tobacco tax rates" (Ambitious Impact's May 2025 review repeats it). No text of the order, date or press report was found (Liberia's executive orders of 2024 and 2025 cover petroleum, farm tariffs and local-industry surcharges), and the finance ministry and the IMF programme Liberia was negotiating in 2024 both pushed for more revenue, not less. This row asks only about the event: that such an order existed, would have taken effect, and didn't. Concentric's part in stopping it is its share of the credit (eo_attribution_share_shared), so the two never ask the same question. One chance (normalization.md 2.18). Our judgment: 25%, from 5% to 60%.

rows.label: Liberia: excise as a share of the price of a pack of cigarettes (2020)

source.title: WHO report on the global tobacco epidemic 2021, country profile: Liberia
source.page: Taxes as a % of price of the most sold brand

rows.explainer: Specific and ad valorem excise together, 46.5% of the most sold brand's US$1.41 pack (VAT, 9.1%, is not excise).

rows.label: Liberia: excise as a share of the price of beer and spirits before 2025
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as Liberia's pre-2025 beverage excise rates and retail prices were not found. The 2025 act set beer's excise at $1.00 a litre; the earlier rates were lower, and were cut further in April 2025. Beverage excise in the region usually makes up a smaller share of the price than tobacco's: 25%, from 10% to 40%, below tobacco's 46.5%.

rows.label: Stopped tax cut: share of the excise the order would have cut
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as the order's rates are unknown: an executive order lowering rates, short of abolishing them, would most likely trim a tenth to a third of the excise. 18%, from 5% to 33%. Used for both tobacco and alcohol.

rows.label: Stopped tax cut: cigarette prices it kept from falling (share)
rows.explainer: The excise's share of the price times the share of it the order would have cut, if fully passed on; weak collection is in the enforcement row.

rows.label: Stopped tax cut: alcohol prices it kept from falling (share)
rows.explainer: The excise's share of the price times the share of it the order would have cut, if fully passed on.

rows.label: Stopped tax cut, alcohol: years the stopped cut counts

source.title: Liberia Revenue Authority, LRA to roll out amended tax laws April 1 (17 March 2025)

rows.explainer: The Legislature cut the excise on beer, wine, other fermented beverages and spirits (HS 2204, 2205, 2206, 2208) from 1 April 2025 (the Liberia Revenue Authority, 17 March 2025; FrontPage Africa, 18 March 2025), about a year after the order would have applied. So the alcohol cut the work stopped came anyway after about a year: 1 year, from 0.5 to 1.5, in place of the site's years for a won reform. Tobacco was not in that amendment and counts the usual years.

rows.label: 2025 tax act: years from the first year's work to the act taking effect

source.title: RegFollower, Liberia enacts Tax Amendment Act, strengthens enforcement and raises excise taxes (2026)

rows.explainer: The act was approved on 24 March 2026 and took effect on its publication in handbills on 1 April 2026 (RegFollower; the Liberia Revenue Authority announced enforcement from 1 April, a secondary report says 1 May), with excise indexed to inflation from 1 January 2027: about two years after the middle of the first year (April 2024), 1.5 to 2.5.

rows.label: 2025 tax act: discounted years counted
2025 tax act: average rise in tobacco prices over the years counted (share)

source.title: RegFollower, Liberia enacts Tax Amendment Act, strengthens enforcement and raises excise taxes (2026)

rows.explainer: Our judgment. The act raises the excise on unmanufactured tobacco to $25 a kilogram and from 2027 indexes the specific excise on tobacco, alcohol and sugary drinks to inflation and growth; the cigarette rate itself was not verified ($0.40 a pack plus ad valorem, by the finance ministry's August 2026 presentation). Indexing stops the specific tax eroding with inflation (Liberia's ran near 10% a year in 2023-24), so over the years counted prices stay a few per cent higher: 3%, from 0.5% to 10%.

rows.label: 2025 tax act: average rise in alcohol prices over the years counted (share)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The act raises the excise on beer to $1.00 a litre and indexes the specific excises from 2027; the earlier rate was not found, and in April 2025 an earlier amendment had cut some beverage excises (FrontPage Africa, 18 March 2025). 6%, from 2% to 15%.

rows.explainer: Liberia's smoking DALYs × the price rise × the share of the burden per unit of price (the elasticity) × the health lag × the years counted, discounted.

rows.label: 2025 tax act: alcohol DALYs averted (before adjustments)

rows.explainer: Liberia's alcohol DALYs × the price rise × the share of the burden per unit of price (the elasticity) × the health lag × the years counted, discounted.

rows.label: Guinea-Bissau: chance its 2022 tobacco tax rise is put into effect in the next few years
rows.explainer: Guinea-Bissau passed higher tobacco taxes in 2022 but, by Concentric's account, had not applied them; Concentric worked with the health ministry and customs on applying them and on a national coordination body (a draft ministerial order validated in November 2024). No sign of either taking effect was found by November 2026, and a military takeover in late 2025 makes government action less predictable. One chance. Our judgment: 12%, from 3% to 30%.

rows.label: Guinea-Bissau: years from the first year's work to the tax applying, if it does
rows.explainer: Nothing applied by late 2026, two and a half years after the middle of the first year: 3 years, from 2 to 5.

rows.label: Guinea-Bissau: discounted years counted
Guinea-Bissau: rise in cigarette prices if the 2022 taxes apply (share)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the 2022 rates were not found and WHO's 2021 profile gives no price or tax share for Guinea-Bissau. A rise toward the regional excise floor (ECOWAS's directive: at least 50% ad valorem and a specific excise) from a low base would raise prices by about a tenth: 10%, from 3% to 25%.

rows.explainer: Guinea-Bissau's smoking DALYs × the price rise × the share of the burden per unit of price (the elasticity) × the health lag × the chance × the years counted, discounted.

rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights for 15 to 49, 50 to 74 (for 50 to 69) and the mean of 70 to 74 and 75 to 79 (for 70 and over, which slightly overvalues deaths at 80 and over), over GBD 2023's deaths by age (shared, facts: death_ages), times how much Your values weigh a life.

rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights for 15 to 49, 50 to 74 (for 50 to 69) and the mean of 70 to 74 and 75 to 79 (for 70 and over, which slightly overvalues deaths at 80 and over), over GBD 2023's deaths by age (shared, facts: death_ages), times how much Your values weigh a life.

rows.explainer: Every death the site counts is valued by the age it happens at (docs/normalization.md, decision 2026-10-31 #4): GiveWell's moral weights for 15 to 49, 50 to 74 (for 50 to 69) and the mean of 70 to 74 and 75 to 79 (for 70 and over, which slightly overvalues deaths at 80 and over), over GBD 2023's deaths by age (shared, facts: death_ages), times how much Your values weigh a life.

rows.explainer: Turns the DALYs back into the deaths behind them (shared, facts: death_ages).

rows.label: Guinea-Bissau: smoking deaths per DALY (GBD 2023)
rows.explainer: Turns the DALYs back into the deaths behind them (shared, facts: death_ages).

rows.label: Alcohol: deaths per DALY
rows.explainer: The same shared figure that turned the deaths into DALYs, turning them back.

rows.label: Tobacco: illness share of the DALYs
rows.explainer: The shared judgment (mostly chronic lung disease); kept as DALYs.

rows.label: Alcohol: illness share of the DALYs
rows.explainer: The shared judgment (mostly alcohol use disorder); kept as DALYs.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with resources others commit only because of it
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): here the government that sets and collects the taxes. The charity is credited this share of the good done; the rest stays with those who carry out the result.

rows.label: Tobacco branches: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The shared figure for tobacco-control wins in low- and middle-income countries (facts: tobacco): only the validity of the effect sizes; few of the price studies are from West Africa.

rows.label: Alcohol branches: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The meta-analysis's elasticities come mostly from rich countries; whether heavy drinkers in Liberia respond as drinkers there do is less sure. 0.7, 0.4 to 1. The untaxed share of drinking is in the enforcement row, not here.

rows.label: Counterfactual adjustment
rows.explainer: 1: whether the change would have come anyway is the years a win counts and, for the stopped order and Guinea-Bissau, each branch's chance; one question (Convention 5).

rows.label: Stopped tax cut: Concentric's share of the credit among those who argued against the order
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the branch's chance (eo_p_success) asks only whether the order was real and stopped; this is Concentric's part in stopping it, among the outside advisers who argued the same (WHO country staff, the IMF team, local health groups). By its own account it worked on it directly with the finance ministry; finance ministry staff who acted on it are credited through the mobiliser's share. 40%, from 20% to 70%.

rows.label: Stopped tax cut: attribution share
rows.explainer: The share among those who did the same work, times the mobiliser's share (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: 2025 tax act: Concentric's share among those who pressed for it
rows.explainer: Our judgment. No source credits Concentric with the act. It worked with the finance ministry on health taxes from 2024 (modelling and writing on health taxes for an IMF loan application, support for an alcohol tax rise it says passed the House of Representatives); WHO economists, the World Bank, the IMF and ECOWAS's excise directive pressed for the same. 4%, from 1% to 12%.

rows.label: 2025 tax act: the first year's share of Concentric's part in it
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the act passed in late 2025, after a second year of Concentric's work in Liberia that the first year's spending didn't pay for. 40%, from 20% to 70%.

rows.label: 2025 tax act: attribution share
rows.explainer: The share among those who pressed for it, times the first year's share of that work, times the mobiliser's share (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Guinea-Bissau: Concentric's share among those working to apply the taxes
rows.explainer: Our judgment: Concentric is one of few outside groups on tobacco control in Guinea-Bissau (its briefs, a memorandum with the health ministry and with customs), beside WHO and the Portuguese tax authority's experts its work brought in. 20%, from 5% to 50%.

rows.label: Guinea-Bissau: the first year's share of Concentric's part, if the taxes apply
rows.explainer: Our judgment: most of the work (the November 2024 mission, the coordination body) came in the second year and more would be needed. 30%, from 15% to 60%.

rows.label: Guinea-Bissau: attribution share
rows.explainer: The share among those doing the same work, times the first year's share, times the mobiliser's share (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Liberia, tobacco: share of a tax change that reaches prices

source.title: Concentric Policies, Marginal funding for the single best health policy in the world (EA Forum post by its founders, November 2024)
source.quote: almost none of the country's tobacco market is paying taxes

rows.explainer: Liberia barely collects tobacco excise: tobacco import excise fell from over $3 million in 2013 to $158,000 in 2022 and $6,000 in 2023 (finance ministry figures in the founders' post), and its own 2025 report to the WHO Framework Convention names weak tobacco tax enforcement as a barrier. Arithmetic, as an illustration: if Liberia's roughly 177,000 smokers (the figure in Concentric's 2024 brief on excise and illicit trade) smoked only five cigarettes a day (our assumption), about 16 million packs a year, excise at 46.5% of a $1.41 pack would come to about $10 million; 2022's and 2023's collections are under 2% of that, 2013's under a third. The founders' own second-year goal was to bring compliance to 25%. So a change in the statutory rate reaches a small part of the market's prices: 10%, from 2% to 30%.

rows.label: Liberia, alcohol: share of a tax change that reaches prices
rows.explainer: Only recorded (taxed) alcohol carries the tax: WHO puts recorded drinking at {{row:lbr_alc_recorded_share}} of Liberia's total (facts: alcohol), the rest home-made cane spirits and other unrecorded drink; times the share of a tax change on recorded drink that reaches its price.

rows.label: Liberia: recorded (taxed) share of alcohol drunk (WHO, 2023)
rows.explainer: Shared (facts: alcohol), from WHO's Global Information System on Alcohol and Health.

rows.label: Liberia, alcohol: share of a tax change on recorded drink that reaches its price
rows.explainer: Our judgment: beer and spirits from the few formal brewers and importers are taxed at the factory or the port, and excise on such goods is usually passed through to prices in full or nearly so (sometimes more). 90%, from 70% to 110%.

rows.label: Guinea-Bissau: share of a tax change that reaches prices
rows.explainer: Weak customs and cross-border trade within the West African customs union leak part of any rise. 50%, from 20% to 80%.

rows.label: Missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12) in every branch: no change in prices, smoking or drinking from Concentric's work is measured, only what the research on such taxes projects.

Side effect, Liberia: second-hand smoke burden averted, as a share of the smoking burden averted
rows.explainer: Fewer smokers means less second-hand smoke for the people around them, which GBD counts apart from smoking, taken as falling in step with smoking and valued with the smokers' ages (which undervalues the children's deaths among it). Liberia: 21,543 DALYs against 27,071 for smoking (facts: tobacco).

rows.label: Side effect, Guinea-Bissau: second-hand smoke burden averted, as a share of the smoking burden averted
rows.explainer: As for Liberia: 6,158 DALYs against 9,439 for smoking (facts: tobacco).

rows.label: Side effect: money smokers' households no longer spend on tobacco, as a share of the value
